title: Constitutional Amendment 4: Legislative Compensation Tied to Median Household Income

context.text: Referred to voters by the New Mexico Legislature as a proposed constitutional amendment; the Secretary of State lists it among four amendments on the November 3, 2026 ballot. A majority of the votes cast on the question is needed to adopt it.

question.text: Proposing to amend Article 4, Section 10 of the Constitution of New Mexico to allow legislative compensation that is limited to the median household income for New Mexico, to require legislative compensation to be reduced if the median household income for New Mexico falls, to allow legislative compensation to be increased only if the median household income for New Mexico rises and to provide for delayed implementation.

summary.text: Entitles legislators to compensation as provided by law, up to an amount equal to the state's annual median household income (about $68,000 in 2026 per the guide), in addition to per diem and mileage, adjusted as median household income rises or falls. It takes effect for members seated for the Fifty-Ninth Legislature in 2029 and removes the current bar on other perquisites or allowances. New Mexico legislators currently receive per diem and mileage but no salary. No fiscal estimate is given in the guide.

measure.yesMeans: Allows the legislature to pay legislators a salary up to the state median household income, effective with the legislature seated in 2029.
measure.noMeans: Keeps legislators unsalaried, receiving only per diem and mileage reimbursement.

argumentsFor.text: Voter guide argument for: "Legislative compensation could result in legislators spending more time on legislative work and less time on outside employment."
Voter guide argument for: "Legislative compensation would diversify the pool of potential legislators."

argumentsAgainst.text: Voter guide argument against: "Legislative salaries could provide legislators with incumbency advantages not available to other candidates."
Voter guide argument against: "The amendment would provide for a legislative salary that is disproportionate when compared to other states."

currentLaw.text: Article 4, Section 10 of the New Mexico Constitution entitles each legislator to per diem (at the IRS rate for Santa Fe) for each day of session and for required interim committee meetings, plus mileage, and says legislators receive "no other compensation, perquisite or allowance." New Mexico legislators therefore receive no salary.

fiscalImpact.text: Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report (Feb. 16, 2026): based on 112 legislators and a median household income of about $67,800, the cost to the general fund could be approximately $7.6 million a year if voters approve; the report shows $3.8 million in FY29 (last half of the fiscal year, when the Fifty-Ninth Legislature is seated) as a recurring cost to the Legislative Council Service, excluding employer payroll taxes and benefits. Putting the question to voters costs the Secretary of State about $35,000 (nonrecurring). The report also notes the Public Employees Retirement Association would have to modify its systems and that retirement contribution and benefit calculations could come to be based on salaries.

supporters.text: Vote for Change, the Albuquerque-based committee backing the amendment
Democratic Party of New Mexico (executive committee voted to support it; chair Sara Attleson)
Resolution sponsors Reps. Parajon, Rubio and Abeyta and Sens. Nava and Charley (House Joint Resolution 5)
The Semilla Project, Somos Un Pueblo Unido and NEA-New Mexico (organized events and canvass training in support, per The New Mexican)

opponents.text: Republican Party of New Mexico (recommends voters oppose it)
Our Values PAC (conservative-leaning committee running opposing ads)
Sen. Pete Campos (D-Las Vegas), who voted against the resolution

campaignFinance.text: Per Oct. 14, 2026 news reports citing campaign finance filings: Vote for Change (supports) had raised just over $3 million since June, including $1.2 million from Western Futures Fund, $800,000 from Contours Inc. and $400,000 from the Center for Civic Action, and had spent $1.1 million on television in early October. The opposing Our Values PAC is a general political committee: its largest 2026-cycle contributor is Peyton Yates at $150,000; a total raised against the amendment was not found. Figures come from the latest reports before the election and may be superseded.

researchNotes: Source: the New Mexico Secretary of State's 2026 Voter Guide and its published ballot question text. The guide reproduces purpose statements and arguments for and against prepared by the legislature (it links nmlegis.gov's Constitutional Amendments 2026 publication) and states that this analysis does not necessarily reflect the Secretary of State's views; arguments are the guide's unattributed summaries, not statements by named campaigns. The Secretary of State says only the title (in capital letters on the joint resolution) appears on the ballot. Required vote: a simple majority. Resolved discrepancy: the HJR 5 text reproduced in the Secretary of State's guide says submission at the 2028 general election, but the enrolled resolution (final text) and the Legislative Finance Committee report say it goes to voters at the next general election (November 2026), after the House Government, Elections and Indian Affairs Committee amendment responded to the Attorney General's concern that 2028 would violate Article XIX; this entry follows the enrolled text and the Secretary of State. Supporters, opponents and finance come from the Santa Fe New Mexican and Albuquerque Journal (Oct. 14, 2026); the New Mexico campaign finance portal itself was not read. The Santa Fe County Clerk's 2026 General Election list of statewide questions includes Constitutional Amendment 4 with the same title, confirming it is on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
